notes:
I've written notes on all 26 verses except v. 21 and v. 25. I found nothing specific on those two that I could check.

Some limits to keep in mind:
- **Sources:** I fully read three pages: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott on BibleHub, and the opening of Precept Austin's page. The tool usage limit then stopped me. For Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and the others below, I only had long search-result extracts.
- **NET Bible notes:** I couldn't read these, except one note on v. 1 that Precept Austin quotes. The NET reading of v. 20 below is its translation, not a note.
- **Denominational differences:** I found no Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican pages that comment on this chapter. I also found no Catholic or Orthodox material on newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and nothing on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are left out rather than guessed.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Whole chapter**
- **Where it fits:** Guzik calls chapters 27–33 Moses' third sermon, and says its theme is covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **The treaty pattern:** Guzik says Deuteronomy follows the pattern of ancient agreements between kings and their subjects, with the LORD as Israel's King. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **A second treaty reading:** Bob Utley (quoted on Precept Austin) also reads the chapter as a royal land-grant treaty. He says Israel had to stay loyal to the covenant to keep the land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **Fulfilment:** Several commentators say Joshua carried out these instructions in Joshua 8:30–35. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/

**v. 1**
- **The elders:** Guzik and Ellicott both note that this is the only place in Deuteronomy where the elders speak alongside Moses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Why the elders:** Precept Austin's explanation is that Moses would not cross the Jordan, but the elders would. They would be responsible for seeing the commands carried out. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **"Keep":** Precept Austin says the Hebrew word suggests guarding, like putting a hedge around something. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **"Today":** Precept Austin also points out that "today" is a key word in chapters 27–34. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **Linking vv. 1–2:** Ellicott suggests the two verses go together: Israel would write the law down in order to keep it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **"All the commandments":** The Pulpit Commentary takes this to mean the whole law Moses had given. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **"On the day":** Gill and Jamieson read this as "about that time," not the exact day of the crossing. Gill notes the ceremony came after Ai was taken. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-27.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **Different stones from Joshua 4:** Gill says these are not the twelve stones taken from the Jordan, which served another purpose. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-27.html
- **The plaster:** It gave a smooth surface so the words could be easily read (Ellicott, Gill). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Written on the plaster:** The Pulpit Commentary argues the words were written on or in the plaster, not carved and then covered. Hiding the words would have defeated the point of a public display. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Background:** Plastered writing stones were an Egyptian technique (Kline, Kalland). The IVP Background Commentary mentions plaster inscriptions found in the region. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/

**v. 3**
- **Law and land:** Ellicott says Israel's right to Canaan depended on keeping God's law as the law of the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **How much was written – a summary:** Gill thinks it was a summary of the laws, perhaps just the Ten Commandments. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-27.html
- **How much was written – the whole law:** The Pulpit Commentary takes it as all the law Moses gave, but probably without the speeches and history around it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-27.html

**v. 4**
- **Mount Ebal:** Gill describes Ebal as dry and rocky. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/27-4.html
- **The "barren" mountain:** Barnes calls Ebal the mountain of "barrenness." He sees it as a fitting place because the curses were the penalties Israel bound itself to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-4.htm
- **Why Ebal and not Gerizim:** Keil and Delitzsch give the same reason the chapter lists only curses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-4.htm
- (The Samaritan "Gerizim" reading is covered in section 3.)

**vv. 5–6**
- **No dressed stone:** Merrill (via Guzik) says uncut stones set Israel's altars apart from Canaanite ones, which used dressed stone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **God's glory, not the stonemason's:** Guzik says God would not share His glory with human skill at His altar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **A picture of Christ:** Gill sees the unhewn altar as a picture of Christ, the stone "cut out without hands." The lack of iron tools means nothing human is added to Christ's sacrifice. Matthew Henry makes a similar point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-4.htm
- **No human help in atonement:** The Pulpit's homilies (Davies, Orr) suggest humans add nothing to atonement, and that art has a lower place in worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-27.html
- **Not the written stones:** Keil and Delitzsch say the altar was not built from the plastered stones. It followed Exodus 20 instead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-4.htm
- **Not from the Jordan:** Ellicott rejects Rashi's idea that the altar stones came from the Jordan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Burnt offerings:** Ellicott says these stand for dedicating one's life to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 7**
- **Peace offerings:** Ellicott calls them thanksgiving for deliverance already given, here the crossing of the Jordan. They were the only offerings the worshipper could eat. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **What the meal meant:** Keil and Delitzsch say the meal let Israel enjoy fellowship with God. The ceremony showed that Israel's blessedness rested on keeping the law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-4.htm
- **Covenant meal:** Pett compares it to the elders' meal at Sinai in Exodus 24:9–11. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/deuteronomy-27.html

**v. 8**
- **"This law":** Ellicott takes it to mean the Ten Commandments.
- **"Plainly":** Ellicott also reports Rashi's tradition that the words were written in "seventy languages." He links this to Pentecost. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **So the people could read it:** The Pulpit Commentary says the point was for the people to know the law easily, citing Habakkuk 2:2. Its homily adds that no priesthood was to keep this knowledge to itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-27.html
- **Making God's word clear:** Guzik applies this to preachers, who should make God's word plain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **The law lasts:** Gill says writing on stone shows the law endures. Christ redeems believers from its curse, but it remains a guide for how they live. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 9**
- **"Be silent":** Ellicott says this Hebrew word appears nowhere else in the Old Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **"This day you have become":** Ellicott says Israel should treat every day as if it were entering the covenant that day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Covenant renewed:** Guzik says the covenant was being formally confirmed with the second generation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Renewing one's commitment:** A Pulpit homily says people "become" the Lord's again when they renew their profession of faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 10**
- **Obedience follows:** Guzik says that if the LORD is King, obedience naturally follows. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Hearing and doing:** Precept Austin connects this to James 1:22, being doers of the word and not only hearers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary

**v. 11**
- **"On that day":** Gill says it refers to the same day Moses gave the orders above. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-27.html

**vv. 12–13**
- **"To bless" and "to curse":** Ellicott says these words mislead. Following the Jewish tract Sotah, the Levites stood between the mountains and spoke, and all the tribes said "Amen." The tribes stood there to receive the blessing or the curse, not to speak it.
- **The altar on Ebal:** Ellicott notes that the law and the altar, which pictures the curse-bearer, are both on Ebal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **How the tribes were split:**
  - The Gerizim tribes are sons of Leah and Rachel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm
  - Ebal has the handmaids' sons, plus Reuben (who lost his birthright, Genesis 49:4) and Zebulun (Leah's youngest). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Seven tribes, in effect:** Ellicott notes that "Joseph" covers Ephraim and Manasseh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **The ark in the valley:** Merrill (via Guzik) notes from Joshua 8:33 that the ark stayed in the valley between the mountains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Why these mountains:** Guzik gives three reasons: the natural amphitheatre, the central location, and Clarke's contrast of fertile Gerizim with barren Ebal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Right and left:** Gill notes Josephus put Gerizim on the right. Gill links this to the final judgment, with the blessed on the right and the cursed on the left. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 14**
- **A chorus of Levites:** The Pulpit Commentary pictures a group of priests chanting together, so no single voice had to carry across the valley. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **"Amen":** Guzik says each Amen meant "so be it," a conscious agreement with the curse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Why no blessings are listed:**
  - The blessings would simply have mirrored the curses (Thompson, via Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
  - They are left out so readers look for blessing in Christ (Trapp, via Guzik; Gill). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm
  - Blessings and curses were probably said alternately (Pulpit). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-27.html

**vv. 15–26 (the twelve curses as a group)**
- **Declarations, not wishes:** Ellicott says the Hebrew has no verb. "Cursed is he" states a fact rather than calling down a curse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Sins named, not curses spelled out:** Guzik says these list sins that stand under God's curse without saying how the curse will fall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Secret sins:** Guzik says many of these sins could escape human courts, but God sees them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Twelve examples:** The Pulpit Commentary says there are twelve, probably one per tribe. They are samples of sins that are easy to hide. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-27.html
- **Ellicott's grouping:**
  - v. 15: idolatry
  - v. 16: parents
  - vv. 17–19: neighbours and the vulnerable
  - vv. 20–23: purity
  - vv. 24–25
  - v. 26: everything
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Secret disobedience:** Pett says these curses fit Ebal because they target secret disobedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/deuteronomy-27.html

**v. 15**
- **The first table of the law:** Gill applies this curse to the first table of the Ten Commandments, the commands about God. He calls worshipping a craftsman's handiwork senseless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 16**
- **Honouring parents:** Ellicott ties this to the first command of the second table. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 17**
- **Boundary stones:** The Biblical Illustrator says moving the "landmarks of faith" is far worse than moving boundary stones. It also applies the verse to honesty in business. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/deuteronomy-27.html

**v. 18**
- **Misleading the "blind":** Rashi (via Ellicott and Gill) widens this to giving bad advice to anyone who is "in the dark" about a matter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Abusing trust:** The Biblical Illustrator applies it to knowingly giving harmful advice and taking advantage of people who trust us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/deuteronomy-27.html

**v. 19**
- **The defenceless:** Gill says these people had no one to take their side, so judges might be tempted to wrong them. God is their protector and avenger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm

**vv. 20–23**
- **Sexual sins in secret:** Gill says these sins were likely done in secret. The people's Amen expressed their horror at them. Gill cross-references Leviticus 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-27.html
- **v. 20 wording:** The NET Bible translates "his father's former wife." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Deu&chapter=27

**v. 24**
- **Secret murder:** Gill reads this as a murder that is never found out, which God's curse still overtakes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Slander:** Rashi (via Ellicott) reads it as backbiting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm

**v. 26**
- **No one escapes:** Guzik says even someone who avoided the other eleven curses cannot keep all the law, so everyone stands under its curse.
- **Hope on Ebal:** Guzik's hope is the altar built on Ebal, the mountain of cursing.
- **The word "all":** Clarke (via Guzik) says printed Hebrew texts lack "all," while the Samaritan text, the Greek Septuagint and Paul in Galatians 3:10 have it.
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Paul's use:** Ellicott says Paul used this verse to argue that no one keeps all the law. Only Christ, who bore Ebal's curse, brings Gerizim's blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **Perfect obedience:** Gill says the law demands perfect and constant obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/27.htm
- **A blessing no sinner can claim:** Orr (Pulpit) says the blessing from Gerizim fails because no sinner can meet its condition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-27.html
- **Applied to all people:** GotQuestions says the New Testament applies this verse to all humanity, because no one keeps the law perfectly. https://www.gotquestions.org/becoming-a-curse-for-us.html

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no sources from different traditions that disagree with each other on this chapter. What I found mostly agrees. Paul uses v. 26 in Galatians 3:10, and it leads to Christ bearing the curse.

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** v. 26 shows God won't "grade on a curve." He demands perfect obedience, and Paul uses the verse to support justification by faith alone. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/christ-our-curse
- **Calvin (on Galatians 3:10):** The law holds everyone under its curse, so it is useless to look to it for blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/3-10.html
- **A different emphasis (Contending for the Faith, on Galatians 3:10):** It says Galatians mainly teaches justified people how to stay justified, rather than teaching an unbeliever how to be justified. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/3-10.html
- **Guzik on the new covenant:** Believers are not under an old-covenant relationship. God does not curse His people, because their punishment fell on Jesus. Guzik still allows for natural consequences of sin and God's correction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-27/
- **Utley:** He stresses that being chosen by God does not replace obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **v. 1:** The NET note says the Hebrew has the singular "commandment." It may stand for the whole law, like the word *torah*. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **v. 1, joined introductions:** The Cambridge Bible suggests two different introductions have been joined here. It also mentions an editor rearranging vv. 2–7 and linking them to the rule of one altar in Deuteronomy 12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-1.htm
- **Out of place?** Block says the chapter seems to interrupt the flow from 26:16–19 into 28:1–14. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-27-commentary
- **Archaeology, vv. 5–6:** Pett mentions a rough stone altar from around Joshua's time found on Mount Ebal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/deuteronomy-27.html
- **Archaeology, a second claim:** A BibleHub article dates a limestone structure on Ebal to the late 13th century BC and cites it as evidence. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Galatians_3_10_curse.htm
- **Why no iron, v. 5:** Pett suggests iron then came mostly from meteorites, linked with other gods, or was imported and "foreign." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/deuteronomy-27.html

**v. 4, the Samaritan reading "Gerizim"**
- **The variant:** The Samaritan Pentateuch reads "Gerizim" instead of "Ebal." Samaritans say theirs is the original and that Ezra changed it. Jewish tradition rejected their claim. https://www.gotquestions.org/Samaritan-Pentateuch.html
- **The older commentators' view:** Gill, Barnes, the Pulpit Commentary, and Keil and Delitzsch treat "Gerizim" as a deliberate change to support the Samaritan temple. They say all Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read "Ebal." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/27-4.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/27-4.html
- **Scholars who disagree:** The Pulpit Commentary notes some critics accept "Gerizim." Coffman objects that the Old Testament scholar Gerhard von Rad reads "Gerizim." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/deuteronomy-27.html

**Catholic**
- **v. 2 (Haydock's Catholic commentary, 1811):** The Latin version of the Samaritan text gives two stones. Haydock takes the law written on them to be just the Ten Commandments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/27-2.html
